lessons.title: Why Cloud AI Platforms?
lessons.chapterTitle: Azure AI Foundry & Cloud AI Concepts

lessons.title: Azure AI Foundry, Overview
lessons.chapterTitle: Azure AI Foundry & Cloud AI Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: Sign in to the Azure AI Foundry portal (ai.azure.com), open or create a project, and browse its model catalog landing page. Then write a short note (3-4 sentences) contrasting the self-hosted code snippet (model = load_model(...); model.generate(prompt)) against the cloud-platform snippet (client = ChatCompletionsClient(endpoint=..., credential=...); client.complete(...)) from the lesson, applied to one specific model you actually see listed in the catalog.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of your real Foundry project's model catalog page, plus a short written note contrasting self-hosted vs. cloud-platform code applied to one real catalog model.

lessons.title: Azure OpenAI Service
lessons.chapterTitle: Azure AI Foundry & Cloud AI Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: In the Azure portal, create a real Azure OpenAI resource (or open an existing one): search for it under Create a resource, fill in Subscription, Resource group, Region, Name, and confirm Standard S0 is the only pricing tier shown. Once it's provisioned, copy its endpoint URL from the Overview page. Then write one sentence explaining, in your own words, why Azure OpenAI routes requests by deployment name instead of letting you pass the model name directly the way OpenAI's own API does.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of your created/open Azure OpenAI resource's Overview page showing its real endpoint, plus a one-sentence explanation of the deployment-name-vs-model-name gotcha.

lessons.title: Model Deployment Options
lessons.chapterTitle: Azure AI Foundry & Cloud AI Concepts

lessons.title: Cloud vs. Self-Hosted Models
lessons.chapterTitle: Azure AI Foundry & Cloud AI Concepts

slots.practicalActivity: In the Foundry model catalog, open the Deployment options filter and compare roughly how many models support Standard (Foundry resource) vs. Serverless API vs. Managed compute. Then, using the lesson's decision checklist (legally_required_on_prem, model_needs_architecture_changes, sustained_usage_beats_token_cost), write a one-paragraph memo for one real scenario of your choosing (e.g. a healthcare app with a strict data-residency requirement) stating whether you'd self-host or use a cloud AI platform, and why.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the catalog filtered by deployment option, plus a one-paragraph decision memo applying the self-host-vs-cloud checklist to a real scenario.

slots.practicalActivity: Without looking back at the lessons, write a one-page Chapter 1 reference sheet covering: the three paths to production (self-hosted, cloud AI platform, fully managed SaaS), the four things a cloud AI platform bundles, the three model deployment options and what actually differs between them, and the four legitimate reasons to self-host. Then check it against the lesson guides and mark any corrections in a different color.
slots.deliverable: A completed one-page Chapter 1 reference sheet with corrections marked in a different color.

slots.practicalActivity: Run pip install azure-identity azure-ai-projects openai. Copy your project's endpoint from its Overview page in the Foundry portal, authenticate with AIProjectClient(endpoint=..., credential=DefaultAzureCredential()), call project.get_openai_client(), and send a real chat completion using your project's actual deployment name as the model argument. Print reply.choices[0].message.content.
slots.deliverable: A runnable Python script that authenticates with DefaultAzureCredential and prints a real chat completion response from your own Foundry project's deployment.

slots.practicalActivity: From the Foundry model catalog, pick a small model, select Use this model, accept terms if a Marketplace step appears, deploy it (Foundry resource deployment or managed compute, your choice), then confirm on the deployment's details page that Provisioning state reads Succeeded and Deployment state reads Healthy. Use the portal's Test tab to send one sample request before writing any application code against it.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of your deployment's details page showing Succeeded and Healthy, plus a successful response from the portal's Test tab.

slots.practicalActivity: Create (or use a free-tier) Azure AI Search service and check its Usage panel for the three-index/indexer/data-source cap. Upload a handful of real text files to an Azure Blob Storage container, then run the no-code Import data wizard to build an index, an indexer, and a data source connection in one pass. Once it finishes, use Search Explorer to run a real query against the finished index.
slots.deliverable: A working Azure AI Search index built via the Import data wizard, with a Search Explorer screenshot showing real results returned for a real query.

slots.practicalActivity: In the Foundry portal's Guardrails and controls 'Try it out' page, run Moderate text content against 3 sample strings of your own choosing (one clearly safe, one mildly offensive, one more severe) and record the severity score (0/2/4/6) each one gets per harm category. Click View Code on one of them and read the exported call it generates.
slots.deliverable: A table of your 3 sample texts with their returned severity scores per harm category, plus the exported View Code snippet for one of them.

slots.practicalActivity: Open Azure Cost Management and use Cost analysis to drill from your subscription down to the specific resource generating the charge (your Azure OpenAI resource or Foundry deployment). Then create a real budget on that resource group with an alert threshold set well below your actual tolerance.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of Cost analysis drilled down to your AI resource's real spend, plus a created budget with a configured alert threshold.

slots.practicalActivity: Open the Monitor tab for your Foundry project and review the operational metrics dashboard (token usage, latency, run success rate charts). Open Monitor settings (the gear icon) and turn on a recurring evaluation, choosing either a scheduled recurrence or a continuous sample of live traffic.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of the Monitor dashboard's operational metrics, plus a configured recurring evaluation (scheduled or continuous).

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Working With Azure AI Services: call your deployed model via the SDK, pass its response through a real Content Safety moderation check, and confirm the call's token usage shows up in Azure Cost Management's Cost analysis and in your Foundry project's Monitor tab.
slots.deliverable: One short script making a real model call and a real moderation check, plus confirmation that the call's usage appears in both Cost Management and the Monitor tab.

lessons.title: Compute Options for AI Workloads: CPU vs. GPU

slots.practicalActivity: Run az vm list-skus --location <your region> --size Standard_NC --output table against your own Azure subscription and record which NC-series sizes are actually sellable there right now. Write one paragraph explaining why an NV-series VM would be the wrong choice for fine-tuning a model, even though its name also implies a GPU.
slots.deliverable: Real CLI output listing available NC-series VM sizes in your region, plus a written paragraph explaining why NV-series is the wrong pick for training.

slots.practicalActivity: Create a Blob Storage container and upload 3-5 real documents into it. Then open your Azure AI Search index's Fields tab from the earlier RAG lesson and identify, by name, which field is the vector field versus which fields are plain text or metadata fields.
slots.deliverable: A populated Blob container with real uploaded documents, plus a written note identifying the vector field vs. the metadata fields in your real search index schema.

slots.practicalActivity: On a real Azure resource (your Key Vault, Storage account, or AI Search service), open its Networking tab and disable public access. Create a private endpoint for it inside a VNet, confirm the connection shows up pending on the resource's Private endpoint connections tab, and approve it.
slots.deliverable: Screenshots showing public access disabled on a real resource, a created private endpoint, and the connection moved from pending to approved.

slots.practicalActivity: On an App Service plan (or similar scalable resource) behind an endpoint, open its Scale out page, switch from Manual scale to Custom autoscale, and write one real scale rule (e.g. average CPU under 20% for 10 minutes -> decrease instance count by one). Write one sentence explaining why that exact CPU-based rule would be the wrong one for a GPU-backed inference endpoint.
slots.deliverable: A configured custom autoscale rule with a real threshold, duration, and action, plus a written explanation of why CPU-based scaling is the wrong signal for GPU inference.

lessons.title: Managed Identities & Key Vault for AI Apps

slots.practicalActivity: Enable a system-assigned managed identity on a real resource (a VM, App Service, or your Foundry project) and confirm Status: On in its Identity blade. Grant that identity an access policy or RBAC role on a real Key Vault. Then write a script that swaps SecretClient(vault_url, credential=ClientSecretCredential(...)) for SecretClient(vault_url, credential=DefaultAzureCredential()) and confirm it can read a real secret with no key anywhere in the code.
slots.deliverable: A confirmed On managed identity, a real Key Vault access grant, and a working script reading a real secret via DefaultAzureCredential with zero hardcoded keys.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending lab for Cloud Infrastructure Basics for AI: take the endpoint you deployed in Chapter 2, put it behind the private endpoint you just created (public access off), move any key it needs into your Key Vault, and confirm the endpoint is still callable, but only from inside your VNet.
slots.deliverable: Your Chapter 2 endpoint secured behind a private endpoint with its key moved into Key Vault, demonstrated reachable only from inside the VNet.

slots.practicalActivity: Sign in to (or sign up for) the AWS Bedrock console, open the model picker, and note at least 3 different model providers listed there (e.g. Amazon, Anthropic, Meta). Run one real aws bedrock-runtime converse CLI call (or use the console's chat playground) against one of those models with a simple prompt.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of Bedrock's model picker showing multiple real providers, plus one real Converse API call and its response.

slots.practicalActivity: Open Google Cloud's Vertex AI Model Garden, search for one real model (e.g. Gemma 3), open its Deploy options, and open the one-click 'Deploy on Vertex AI' configuration pane. Note what it asks you to choose (region, machine spec, GPU type) without necessarily completing the deployment.
slots.deliverable: A screenshot of a real Model Garden search result and its Deploy on Vertex AI configuration pane.

slots.practicalActivity: Build a 3-row comparison table across Azure AI Foundry/Azure OpenAI, AWS Bedrock, and Vertex AI/Model Garden against the lesson's four real decision questions (where's the data, who's already on which cloud, which models does each platform actually offer, what does the team already know) for one real or hypothetical project. Then write one small Python function ask_model(prompt) that wraps your current Azure call, demonstrating the single-seam pattern that would make swapping providers later a one-function change instead of a codebase-wide hunt.
slots.deliverable: A 3-cloud comparison table against the four real decision questions, plus a working ask_model() wrapper function isolating your current provider call behind one seam.

slots.practicalActivity: Chapter-ending practice for Multi-Cloud AI Awareness: write a one-page 'cloud AI platform decision memo' for a real or hypothetical project, naming which of the three clouds you'd pick, citing the specific one of the four decision factors that actually tipped it, and listing the three portability habits (prompts in files, config in environment variables, embedding dimension/distance metric noted explicitly) you'd follow from day one regardless of which cloud you picked.
slots.deliverable: A completed one-page decision memo naming a specific deciding factor and the three portability habits you'd follow.

slots.practicalActivity: Pick the specific model and deployment option (managed compute or serverless, your own VM quota or the 168-hour shared-quota checkbox) you'll use for your capstone endpoint, and write 2-3 sentences stating your choice and why it's realistically something you can finish, favoring the smallest model and simplest option that still gives you a real Target URI.
slots.deliverable: A short written capstone plan naming your chosen model, deployment option, and quota source.

lessons.title: Capstone: Deploying a Model Endpoint on Azure

slots.practicalActivity: Run the real 5-step SDK flow against your own Foundry project: authenticate with MLClient and InteractiveBrowserCredential, create a ManagedOnlineEndpoint, deploy a real model from the catalog into it as a ManagedOnlineDeployment, route 100% of traffic to it, then confirm Provisioning state Succeeded and Deployment state Healthy, and invoke it with a real request file.
slots.deliverable: A live endpoint confirmed Succeeded and Healthy, with a successfully invoked real request/response and the Target URI saved for the next lesson.

slots.practicalActivity: Move your endpoint's key into a real Key Vault secret and confirm DefaultAzureCredential() can read it with no key hardcoded anywhere. Then run the real az monitor diagnostic-settings create command against your endpoint resource's ID, pointed at a Log Analytics workspace, and confirm the diagnostic setting exists.
slots.deliverable: A Key Vault secret readable via DefaultAzureCredential with no hardcoded key, plus a confirmed diagnostic setting sending logs to Log Analytics.

slots.practicalActivity: Deliver a real 5-minute walkthrough (recorded, or live to a peer) covering: the model you deployed and why, your Target URI live and Healthy, one real security control shown working (DefaultAzureCredential reading your Key Vault secret), and your diagnostic setting. Name one honest, specific limitation of your deployment (e.g. single instance, no autoscaling) instead of claiming it's production-ready. Afterward, delete the deployment (or let the shared-quota 168-hour timer do it) to stop billing.
slots.deliverable: A 5-minute capstone walkthrough naming one honest limitation, plus confirmation the deployment was deleted or scheduled to auto-delete afterward.

slots.practicalActivity: Final review for Azure AI & Cloud for AI Engineers: without notes, explain out loud the difference between an endpoint and a deployment, why Azure OpenAI uses deployment names instead of model names, what a managed identity buys you over a hardcoded key, and the four real factors for choosing between Azure, AWS, and Google's AI platforms. Organize your capstone proof (Succeeded/Healthy screenshot, Key Vault read, diagnostic setting) somewhere you can show it in an interview.
slots.deliverable: A completed, notes-free self-review covering all five chapters, plus your saved capstone proof organized for portfolio use.

monthlyMilestoneContribution: After this course, a student can deploy, secure, and monitor a real model endpoint in Azure AI Foundry end to end using the SDK, Key Vault-backed managed identities, private networking, and diagnostic logging, and can knowledgeably compare that workflow against AWS Bedrock and Google Vertex AI.
